## Parallelism Strategies for Distributed Training {#sec-ch4}

*Who Holds What, and Who Talks to Whom*

### Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- State the single-device baseline every parallelism strategy modifies,
  and the batch-size relation it already establishes before any device
  is added.
- For a given strategy, state what is replicated and what is sharded,
  and whether its communication is a collective operation or a
  point-to-point transfer.
- Distinguish data parallelism from ZeRO/FSDP-style sharded data
  parallelism, and state precisely what sharding changes (residency,
  communication pattern) versus what it does not change (the training
  objective).
- Distinguish intra-layer partitioning (tensor parallelism) from
  inter-layer partitioning (pipeline parallelism), and state why
  pipeline parallelism is not "data parallelism spread across batches."
- Distinguish context/sequence parallelism from both tensor and
  pipeline parallelism, and distinguish expert placement (a
  distributed-systems decision) from sparse expert activation (an
  architecture decision, Workbook 04's domain).
- Given a target world size, factor it across parallelism dimensions,
  verify the factorization is valid, and identify one representative
  rank's process-group membership on each axis.

### Why this matters

Workbook 04 chapter 7's own parallelism table explicitly deferred its
derivation to "a future training workbook" — this chapter keeps that
promise. Every strategy in this chapter answers the same underlying
question: given a model and a cluster, what gets copied onto every
device, what gets split across devices, and which devices need to
talk to which other devices to keep the math correct? No single
strategy scales without limit, so production training runs combine
several of them at once — getting the combination right requires
knowing exactly what each one partitions, not just that it "helps with
memory" or "helps with speed." This chapter stays at the level of what
is partitioned, replicated, and communicated; Chapter 5 covers the
memory accounting, communication-volume analysis, and throughput
tradeoffs that follow from these choices.

### Mental model or analogy

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy"}
Picture a huge banquet kitchen. A single station is the single-device
baseline. **Data parallelism** adds identical stations, each cooking
the full recipe for a different set of tables, occasionally comparing
notes so every station's recipe stays in sync. **Tensor parallelism**
instead splits *one dish's preparation* across several cooks *at the
same station*, working on the same order simultaneously and talking
constantly to combine their parts. **Pipeline parallelism** is an
assembly line: one station handles appetizers, the next handles
mains, the next handles dessert, and orders move down the line.
**Expert parallelism** is a set of specialist chefs — a sushi chef, a
pastry chef — who only get called on for the orders that need their
specialty, and sit idle otherwise. **Where this breaks down:** real
GPUs synchronize at the level of exact numerical tensors, not casual
notes, and a single training step usually uses *several* of these
arrangements at once, sliced along different axes of the *same* set
of devices — not one kitchen choosing one arrangement.
:::

### Technical core

**Single-device baseline.** Before adding any device, a single GPU
already has two batch-size-related knobs: the **micro-batch size**
(`mbs`, how many samples fit through one forward/backward pass) and
**gradient accumulation** (`grad_acc` passes' gradients summed, then
averaged, before one optimizer step). This gives the baseline relation

$$
\text{bs} = \text{gbs} = \text{mbs} \times \text{grad\_acc}
$$ {#eq-single-device-batch}

[@src-17] — the **global batch size** (`gbs`) a single device can
reach by trading compute time for a larger effective batch, at
constant memory. Every parallelism strategy below either adds a new
term to this equation or changes what a "device" running one term of
it actually holds.

**Data parallelism (DP): full replication, sharded data.** Data
parallelism copies the **entire model** onto every worker and gives
each worker a **different** micro-batch. Since each worker computes
different gradients, an **all-reduce** — a collective operation
summing (and then averaging) the gradients across all DP ranks —
synchronizes them before the optimizer step [@src-17]. Nothing about
the model or its parameters is sharded; only the *data* is. Adding a
DP degree updates the global batch relation:

$$
\text{gbs} = \text{mbs} \times \text{grad\_acc} \times \text{dp}
$$ {#eq-dp-global-batch}

[@src-17]. In practice, teams maximize `dp` before adding gradient
accumulation, since DP ranks run in parallel while accumulation steps
run sequentially [@src-17].

**ZeRO / FSDP-style sharded data parallelism: same objective, different
residency.** Vanilla DP replicates optimizer states, gradients, and
parameters on every rank — a real memory redundancy. ZeRO removes this
redundancy by **partitioning** (not replicating) these objects across
the DP ranks, in three cumulative stages, using the original paper's
own notation ($\Psi$ = parameter count, $N_d$ = DP degree)
[@src-54;@src-17]:

- **ZeRO-1** ($P_{os}$): shards only the **optimizer states**.
- **ZeRO-2** ($P_{os+g}$): shards optimizer states **and gradients**.
- **ZeRO-3 / FSDP** ($P_{os+g+p}$): shards optimizer states, gradients,
  **and parameters**.

"ZeRO-3" (DeepSpeed's name) and "FSDP" (PyTorch's name) are the *same*
mechanism under two different names, per the Ultra-Scale Playbook's
own explicit equivalence statement [@src-17] — not two different
techniques. ZeRO-1/2 change the gradient-synchronization collective
from all-reduce to **reduce-scatter**, plus an **all-gather** to
restore full parameters after the optimizer step; ZeRO-3 additionally
all-gathers each layer's parameters on demand during the forward and
backward pass, discarding them immediately after use [@src-17]. The
ZeRO paper's own framing is precise about what this buys you: ZeRO-DP
"achieves the computation/communication efficiency of \[data
parallelism\] while achieving memory efficiency of \[model
parallelism\]" by **partitioning model states instead of replicating
them**, while **retaining the computational granularity and
communication volume of DP** [@src-54]. Sharding changes *where each
piece of the model state lives* and *what gets communicated and when*
— it does not change the mathematical training objective being
optimized.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"Sharding parameters with ZeRO/FSDP changes what the model computes."**
It does not. Every ZeRO stage still computes the same forward pass,
the same loss, and the same gradients as vanilla DP — sharding only
changes which device stores which slice of the optimizer states,
gradients, or parameters at rest, and which collective operation
(all-reduce vs. reduce-scatter-plus-all-gather) reconstructs the full
values when they are needed [@src-54;@src-17].
:::

**Tensor parallelism (TP): intra-layer partitioning.** Tensor
parallelism splits **individual matrix operations within a layer**
across ranks — an *intra-layer* partition, unlike DP or PP which never
split a single operation. For a linear layer $Y = XW$, a weight matrix
can be split by columns (**column-parallel**: broadcast the input,
split $W$'s columns, combine the per-rank outputs with an
**all-gather**) or by rows (**row-parallel**: split the input with a
**scatter**, split $W$'s rows, combine the partial sums with an
**all-reduce**) [@src-53;@src-17]. In a transformer block, the
efficient layout is column-parallel then row-parallel for the MLP —
needing only one all-reduce in the forward pass and one in the
backward pass — and the same column-then-row pattern for
attention: $Q$, $K$, $V$ projections are column-parallel (each rank
computes a subset of attention heads), and the output projection is
row-parallel [@src-53]. Combining both blocks this way needs "only two
all-reduces in the forward path and two in the backward path" per
transformer layer, per Megatron-LM's own count [@src-53]. **A real
divisibility constraint:** the TP degree must not exceed, and should
evenly divide, the number of key/value heads, since each rank needs
whole attention heads to compute independently — for example, Llama-3
8B has 8 K/V heads, so its TP degree should not exceed 8 [@src-17].

A closely related technique, **sequence parallelism (SP)**, is easy to
conflate with a different technique also sometimes called "sequence
parallelism" — the Ultra-Scale Playbook flags this explicitly: SP in
this (TP-coupled) sense splits the operations TP does *not* shard
(LayerNorm, dropout) along the **sequence** dimension, and is *always*
used together with TP; the *other* technique sometimes given the same
name is what this chapter calls **context parallelism** below, which
can be used independently of TP [@src-17]. Treat these as two
different techniques that happen to share a name, not one technique
under two names.

**Context parallelism (CP): sharding activations along the sequence
dimension, everywhere.** Where SP only shards the non-TP operations,
CP shards the **input sequence itself across the entire model**,
including the parts TP already shards [@src-17]. Most modules (MLP,
LayerNorm) process each token independently and are unaffected: no
extra communication is needed there, since only inputs — not weight
matrices — are split [@src-17]. The exception is the **attention**
module, where each token needs key/value pairs from other tokens in
the sequence. **Ring Attention** handles this with **point-to-point**
transfers rather than a single collective: each rank sends its
current key/value chunk to the next rank in a ring (non-blocking),
computes attention on whatever chunk it currently holds, and receives
the next chunk from the previous rank, repeating until every rank has
seen every chunk [@src-17]. A naive ring assignment causes load
imbalance under causal masking (the rank holding the earliest tokens
finishes sooner than the rank holding the latest tokens); **zig-zag**
ring attention reassigns chunks so every rank does comparable work
[@src-17]. After gradients are computed, CP synchronizes them across
the CP group with an ordinary all-reduce, the same as DP [@src-17].

**Pipeline parallelism (PP): inter-layer partitioning.** Pipeline
parallelism splits the model's **layers** — not any single operation —
across devices: for example, a first device holds layers 1 through 4,
a second holds layers 5 through 8, and so on [@src-17]. This is an
*inter-layer* partition, the opposite axis from TP's intra-layer
split. GPipe's own formalism: a sequence of $L$ layers is partitioned
into $K$ cells placed on $K$ accelerators, and a mini-batch of size $N$
is split into $M$ micro-batches that are pipelined through the $K$
accelerators; gradients from all $M$ micro-batches are accumulated and
applied together at the end, so the resulting parameter update is
numerically the same regardless of how many partitions are used
[@src-52].

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"Pipeline parallelism is just data parallelism spread across
consecutive batches."** It is not. In DP, every rank holds an
*identical, full* model and synchronizes *gradients* via all-reduce.
In PP, each stage holds a *different, partial* slice of the model's
layers and passes *activations* (not gradients, not full replicas)
**point-to-point** to its neighboring stage [@src-17]. A PP stage
cannot compute a full forward pass alone — it depends on the previous
stage's output — which is never true of a DP rank.
:::

Naively running one micro-batch at a time through all stages leaves
most devices idle most of the time, an effect GPipe's own paper coined
the **bubble overhead** [@src-52]. A pipeline schedule has three
phases: a **fill** phase (early stages start work before later stages
have anything to do yet), a **steady-state** phase (every stage
processing some microbatch), and a **drain** phase (mirroring fill, as
the last microbatches finish). GPipe's own guideline: bubble overhead
becomes negligible once the number of microbatches $M$ is at least
$4 \times K$ (the number of pipeline stages) [@src-52]. The simplest
schedule, **all-forward-all-backward (AFAB)**, runs every microbatch's
forward pass before any backward pass begins; **one-forward-one-backward
(1F1B)** instead starts each microbatch's backward pass as soon as
possible, which does not shrink the bubble itself but needs to hold
far fewer microbatches' activations in memory at once [@src-17]. The
figure below shows 1F1B's fill/steady-state/drain shape and where its
bubbles fall:

![A schematic one-forward-one-backward (1F1B) pipeline schedule for 4
stages and 6 microbatches, computed programmatically from the standard
1F1B algorithm. Notice the fill phase (upper-left, forward-only),
steady state (the diagonal band alternating forward and backward), and
drain phase (lower-right, backward-only) — with idle bubble slots
outside the diagonal
band.](figures/rendered/fig-pipeline-timeline.svg){#fig-pipeline-timeline}

More recent schedules (interleaved stages, ZeroBubble, DeepSeek-V3's
DualPipe) push the bubble further down by splitting the backward pass
itself into finer-grained pieces that can be rescheduled independently
[@src-17] — the qualitative existence of fill/steady-state/drain and
bubbles is this chapter's subject; the quantitative bubble-time
formulas and schedule comparisons are Chapter 5's.

**Expert parallelism (EP): placement and routing, not architecture.**
Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models replace a single feedforward module
with several parallel expert modules and route each token to one or a
few of them — that architectural routing decision is Workbook 04's
subject, not this chapter's. **Expert parallelism** is the
*distributed-systems* decision of **where each expert lives**: since
each expert's feedforward layer is independent, EP simply places
different experts on different devices, then uses an **all-to-all**
collective to send each token's hidden state to the device holding its
assigned expert (and another all-to-all to gather the results back)
[@src-17]. This is lighter-weight than TP, since no single matrix
multiplication is split — only routing changes. EP alone does not
shard the non-MoE layers or the input tokens, so it is normally
combined with DP: DP shards the batch, EP shards the experts
[@src-17]. A real routing constraint: DeepSeek-V3's router enforces
that each token is sent to at most 4 nodes, keeping traffic within a
smaller physical neighborhood to reduce communication overhead
[@src-17].

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"A higher expert-parallelism degree means the model activates more
experts per token."** It does not. EP degree is about **how many
devices the existing set of experts is spread across** — a placement
decision. How many experts each token actually activates (sparse
routing) is a property of the model's own router, fixed by its
architecture regardless of how those experts happen to be distributed
across devices [@src-17].
:::

**Multidimensional composition: DP x TP x PP x CP x EP.** These axes
are designed to compose: the total number of devices used is the
**product** of the per-axis degrees actually in use,

$$
\text{world\_size} = \text{dp} \times \text{tp} \times \text{pp} \times \text{cp} \times \text{ep}
$$ {#eq-world-size-factorization}

with any axis not in use simply set to 1. Compatibility constraints
apply per axis (e.g. TP bounded by, and dividing, the K/V head count;
EP only meaningful when MoE layers exist), and not every model needs
every dimension — the Ultra-Scale Playbook is explicit that "none of
these techniques is a silver bullet for magical scaling," and that
combining them is a deliberate choice, not a default [@src-17]. Two
axes are worth contrasting directly since they are easy to conflate:
PP and ZeRO-3 both partition "the model" along its depth and both
avoid replicating full parameters — but PP's inter-stage communication
moves **activations** point-to-point between neighbors, while ZeRO-3's
communication **gathers weights** via collectives as needed, and each
PP stage still computes with a **full layer**, while ZeRO-3 ranks
compute with only a **fraction** of a layer's parameters materialized
at once [@src-17]. TP is typically kept within a single node (fast
intra-node interconnect), while PP and ZeRO-3 more readily span slower
inter-node connections [@src-17].

### Worked example

**A 64-device, four-axis layout.** Take a target world size of 64
devices, illustrative only, and choose $\text{dp}=4$, $\text{tp}=4$,
$\text{pp}=2$, $\text{ep}=2$. Since $4 \times 4 \times 2 \times 2 = 64$
matches the world size, this is a valid factorization
(@eq-world-size-factorization). Fixing the rank-decomposition
convention as DP (outermost) > PP > TP > EP (innermost), rank $r$
decodes as

$$
\text{ep\_idx} = r \bmod \text{ep}, \quad
\text{tp\_idx} = \left\lfloor \frac{r}{\text{ep}} \right\rfloor \bmod \text{tp}, \quad
\text{pp\_idx} = \left\lfloor \frac{r}{\text{ep} \times \text{tp}} \right\rfloor \bmod \text{pp}, \quad
\text{dp\_idx} = \left\lfloor \frac{r}{\text{ep} \times \text{tp} \times \text{pp}} \right\rfloor
$$

For representative rank $r = 37$, this gives
$(\text{dp\_idx}, \text{pp\_idx}, \text{tp\_idx}, \text{ep\_idx}) = (2, 0, 2, 1)$,
computed programmatically:

| Group (varying axis) | Member ranks | Group size |
|---|---|---|
| DP group (dp\_idx varies) | 5, 21, 37, 53 | 4 |
| TP group (tp\_idx varies) | 33, 35, 37, 39 | 4 |
| PP group (pp\_idx varies) | 37, 45 | 2 |
| EP group (ep\_idx varies) | 36, 37 | 2 |

: Process-group membership for representative rank 37, in a 64-device DP=4/TP=4/PP=2/EP=2 layout — every group correctly contains rank 37 itself, verified programmatically {#tbl-rank37-groups}

This layout puts $\text{world\_size} / \text{dp} = 64 / 4 = 16$ devices
behind each of the 4 data-parallel replicas, matching
$\text{tp} \times \text{pp} \times \text{ep} = 4 \times 2 \times 2 = 16$
exactly. **This one valid layout is not a claim that it is the fastest
or most memory-efficient choice for any real model** — it exists to
show the factorization and rank-decomposition method, which Chapter
5's cost analysis would need to actually compare against alternatives.

**Global batch size.** With $\text{dp}=4$ from this layout, a
micro-batch size of 2 and 8 gradient-accumulation steps per optimizer
step give

$$
\text{gbs} = 2 \times 8 \times 4 = 64
$$

(@eq-dp-global-batch), distinct from the micro-batch size (2) and the
per-rank local batch across one accumulation cycle
($2 \times 8 = 16$, still smaller than the global batch since it does
not yet include the DP multiplier).

**Invalid configurations, checked programmatically.** Two configurations that fail validation and must be rejected before use:

- $\text{dp}=3, \text{tp}=4, \text{pp}=2, \text{ep}=2$ against a 64-device
  world size: $3 \times 4 \times 2 \times 2 = 48 \ne 64$ — an invalid
  factorization.
- $\text{tp}=3$ against a model with 8 key/value heads: $8 \bmod 3 \ne 0$ —
  an invalid divisibility, since 3 ranks cannot each hold a whole
  number of the 8 heads.

Both are confirmed to raise a validation error, and the valid
configuration ($\text{tp}=4$ against 8 K/V heads, $8 \bmod 4 = 0$) is
confirmed *not* to raise one.

### Compare and contrast

| Aspect | DP | Sharded DP | TP | PP | CP | EP |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Partitioned | Micro-batches | Opt. states (+grad/+params) | Matrix ops in a layer | Model layers | Sequence/activations | Expert FFN modules |
| Replicated | Full model | DP's compute; residency differs | Non-sharded ops | Full layer per stage | Non-attention modules | Non-MoE layers |
| Communication | All-reduce (grad) | Reduce-scatter + all-gather | All-reduce/all-gather | Point-to-point (activations) | Point-to-point ring (K/V) | All-to-all (routing) |
| Motivation | More throughput/batch | Remove DP's redundant state memory | Fit oversized layer weights | Fit oversized model depth | Fit long sequences | Scale expert capacity |
| Key constraint | Needs large enough batch | Comms scale with depth | TP $\le$ K/V heads, divides evenly | Needs $M \gtrsim 4K$ microbatches | Needs long-enough sequence | Needs enough experts/MoE layers |
| Misconception | "More DP always helps" | "Sharding changes the math" | "TP is free parallelism" | "PP = DP over batches" | "CP and SP are the same" | "Higher EP = more active experts" |

: Six parallelism strategies compared on what each partitions and replicates, not on which is fastest or most memory-efficient in general — those depend on model shape, sequence length, and hardware, per [@src-17]'s own qualification. Each misconception is stated in full, with its correction, earlier in this chapter's Technical core. {#tbl-parallelism-compare}

### Applied exercise

For a target world size of 128 devices, choose $\text{tp}=8$,
$\text{pp}=4$, and $\text{ep}=2$. Compute the implied data-parallel
degree from @eq-world-size-factorization, confirm the four degrees'
product equals 128, and state how many devices form one complete
model replica. Then, using a micro-batch size of 1 and 16
gradient-accumulation steps, compute the resulting global batch size
from @eq-dp-global-batch. Check your own arithmetic the same way this
chapter's worked example was checked: verify the product of all four
parallelism degrees equals the world size before trusting the
resulting global batch size.

### Interview lens

*"Given a fixed cluster, how would you decide which parallelism
strategies to combine for training a large model?"* A strong answer
starts from the single-device baseline and names the actual bottleneck
each strategy relieves — DP for throughput and global batch, ZeRO/FSDP
for redundant model-state memory, TP for weights too large for one
device (bounded by K/V head count), PP for models too deep for one
device, CP for sequences too long for one device's attention memory,
EP for the number of experts a MoE architecture needs to place. A
complete answer also states the resulting world-size factorization
explicitly (@eq-world-size-factorization) and checks it multiplies out
correctly, and distinguishes which axes need fast intra-node bandwidth
(TP) from which tolerate slower inter-node links (PP, ZeRO-3, EP). An
answer that recommends "just use all five dimensions" without stating
which bottleneck each one addresses, or that claims one fixed
combination is universally best, is incomplete — per the Ultra-Scale
Playbook's own caution, none of these techniques is a silver bullet,
and not every model needs every dimension [@src-17].

### Chapter recap

- Every parallelism strategy either replicates or shards some object
  (data, optimizer states, gradients, parameters, activations, or
  experts); naming which one is the first step in understanding any
  strategy, starting from the single-device batch-size relation
  (@eq-single-device-batch).
- ZeRO/FSDP shards model state across the DP group in three cumulative
  stages (optimizer states; +gradients; +parameters) and changes
  residency and communication pattern, not the mathematical training
  objective [@src-54;@src-17].
- Tensor parallelism (intra-layer) and pipeline parallelism
  (inter-layer) partition along different axes and use different
  communication patterns — TP's all-reduce/all-gather sits inside a
  layer's computation; PP's point-to-point activation transfer sits
  between stages holding different layers, which is why PP is not
  "data parallelism over consecutive batches" [@src-53;@src-52;@src-17].
- Context parallelism shards the sequence across the whole model using
  point-to-point ring communication for attention specifically, and is
  usable independently of TP — unlike TP-coupled sequence parallelism,
  which shares a name but is a different, always-TP-paired technique
  [@src-17].
- Expert parallelism places experts across devices and routes tokens
  to them via all-to-all; it is a distributed-placement decision,
  distinct from the architecture's own sparse-routing decision (how
  many experts a token activates), which remains Workbook 04's subject
  [@src-17].
- These axes compose multiplicatively into the total world size
  (@eq-world-size-factorization), subject to real divisibility and
  compatibility constraints — not every model needs every dimension,
  and no single combination is universally fastest or most
  memory-efficient [@src-17].

### Sources and further reading

Primary sources for this chapter: [@src-17] (the Ultra-Scale
Playbook's Data Parallelism, ZeRO, Tensor Parallelism, Sequence
Parallelism, Context Parallelism, Pipeline Parallelism, Expert
Parallelism, and "5D parallelism in a nutshell" sections — verified
via full-text extraction of the article's own markdown source),
[@src-52] (GPipe's Sections 1-2 — the pipeline-cell formalism,
synchronous micro-batch gradient accumulation, and the paper's own
coined "bubble overhead" term — verified via full-text extraction of
the arXiv PDF), [@src-53] (Megatron-LM's Section 3 — the column/row
tensor-parallel split for MLP and self-attention blocks, and its
own two-all-reduces-per-layer count — verified via full-text extraction
of the arXiv PDF), and [@src-54] (the ZeRO paper's Sections 1 and 5 —
the $P_{os}$/$P_{os+g}$/$P_{os+g+p}$ stage notation and its own
"computation/communication efficiency of DP, memory efficiency of MP"
framing — verified via full-text extraction of the arXiv PDF). This
chapter deliberately does not reteach Mixture-of-Experts architecture
or routing itself — that is Workbook 04's domain; this chapter treats
expert parallelism only as a placement and communication strategy.
Detailed memory accounting, communication-volume analysis, overlap
strategies, and throughput tradeoffs for all of these strategies are
Chapter 5's subject, not this chapter's.
